text: The assembly will hear an address by His
Excellency Christian Mskosski, President
of the Government of the Republic of
North Macedonia.
I request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to address the
assembly.
Mr. President,
Mr. Secretary General, excellencies,
ladies and gentlemen,
a child
who will sit at a school desk for the
first time this autumn will in 2040 be a
young person just entering adulthood.
We do not know exactly what the world in
which that young person will live will
look like. But we already know that it
will be a different from our own.
Artificial intelligence will transform
professions, industries, and the ways in
which decisions are made. Energy will be
governed by a new configuration and a
new logic of operation. Climate change
will affect economies, agriculture,
cities, and the movement of people.
Demographic change will reshape labor
markets and social protection systems.
Security will no longer depend on armies
and borders, but also on power grids,
data centers, cables, satellites,
algorithms, and trust in the information
we receive every day. And yet today, as
we prepare for the future, millions of
people are living through war or under
the threat of war. More than 100 million
people have been displaced by force.
More than 270
million children and young people are
not in the school. This is the paradox
of our time. Humanity has never
possessed such immense scientific and
technological capabilities.
And yet it has never been more evident
that technological capability does not
automatically produce political wisdom.
That is why the real question before
this assembly is not simply how we will
manage the crisis of 2026.
The real question is this. What kind of
international order will leave to the
generations that is entering school
today?
For a smallsized country like mine, this
is not an academic question. It is a
question of survival.
33 years ago, since we become a part of
the United Nations, the world looked
very different. The Cold War had ended.
There was hope that a new era was
beginning, an era in which cooperation
would gradually replace confrontation.
Our region, however, was living through
a very different reality. Yugoslavia was
disintegrating in bloodshed. Wars were
being fought just beyond our borders.
The fear that the violence might spread
was real. And yet my country choose
peace. It choose stability.
It was in those circumstances on our
territory that the United Nations did
something it had never done before. It
established the first preventive
peacekeeping mission in the history of
the organization.
That experience left a profound lesson
in our national memory. A lesson to
which I will return towards the end of
my speech.
Peace does not begin when war ends.
Peace begins when politics is wise
enough to prevent war from beginning.
Perhaps that is why small countries
sometimes see international politics
differently. Great powers have room for
strategic shifts that small-sized states
simply do not have.
For a great power, a mistaken
geopolitical calculation may mean a
change of a strategy. For a small-sized
country, the same mistake can mean a
lost decade.
That is why we cannot afford to be
indifferent to the rules. Nor can we
afford to believe that the rules will
defend themselves.
The world taking shape before us is a
world of sharper competition. Power is
being redistributed.
Relations among the major power
increasingly shaped trade. technology,
energy, critical raw minerals, transport
routes, and digital infrastructure.
What we called economic interdependence
yesterday, we increasingly see today as
a matter of national security.
Globalization is not disappearing, it is
being reshaped.
Supply chain are changing. Production is
once again becoming a geopolitical
question.
States are asking not only where
something can be produced most cheaply,
but who can be trusted. Not only where
energy comes from, but whether it will
be available when crisis strikes. Not
only who develops the next generation of
technology, but who will set the rules
under which it will operate. alliances
to are changing under the pressure of
this same world. Macedonian citizens
know where they belong. We are a NATO
ally. The United States are our
strategical partner. Full membership in
the European Union is our strategic
commitment.
These are not three separate policies.
They are one geopolitical orientation,
an orientation grounded in democracy,
collective security, the rule of law,
and an open economy. In a time of
uncertaintity, our response is not
strategic ambiguity. Our response is
clarity. But clarity in our alliances
does not mean turning away from the
world. Quite the opposite. It is a
precisely state that is confident in its
democratic and strategic choices that
can engage and cooperate with greater
confidence with countries that have
different histories, different interests
and different political perspectives.
The world does not need yet another
division into permanent camps. It needs
competition with limits and rules that
all must respect. Alliances that take
responsibility and international
institutions that remain a space for a
dialogue precisely when dialogue is most
difficult. That is why the United
Nations matters. Not because they can
resolve every conflict. Clearly they
cannot. Not because every resolution is
given effect. Clearly, that is not
always the case. And that should not
discourage us. It should strengthen our
determination to protect this United
Nations and the rules upon which they
are founded and to stand for
multilateralism grounded in values,
mutual respect, and rules. Because a
world without a place where all states,
regardless of their size, can sit under
the same roof and invoke the same
principles, would be even more dangerous
than the world we see today.
In 1954, Duck Hammershelt reminded us of
a thought. The United Nations were not
created to take us to heaven, but to
save us from hell.
Seven decades later, it is worth
understanding the essence of that
statement. We should not demand
perfection from United Nations. We
should demand relevance, the capacity to
prevent and to mediate, the capacity to
protect human dignity, and ultimately
the capacity to uphold principles even
when applying them is politically
inconvenient.
Today, trust in the international system
in being jeopardized precisely because
too many people have a justified sense
that the rules do not apply equally,
that power sometimes take precedence
over principle, that commitments are
conditional,
that agreements last only as long as
interest remain unchanged.
For small-siz states, this is an
especially dangerous world.
Our own history has taught us that
international compromises are very
difficult and that peace, stability, and
integration require political courage
and hard sacrifices.
And without wishing to sound
patronizing,
if anyone wants to see an example of a
country that has repeatedly given up
something that naturally belongs to it
as a fundamental right, something that
many take for granted. All they need is
to look at the recent history of my
nation.
A history marked by challenges, by
security risks of regional proportions,
by constant compromises and concessions
made in the name of peace and
cooperation and the higher goal of
integration, often at the expense of
most basic understanding of dignity and
justice. We have taken truly difficult
decisions. We have continued forward
even when processes lasted longer than
one generation of citizens could
reasonably have expected.
But precisely for that reason with the
benefit of distance from those decisions
and with a clear awareness of reality I
can responsibly say today that trust
cannot be a one-way obligation
indefinitely.
If small-siz states are expected to
comply with the rules, then the rules
must also provide them with
predictability. If candidates for
membership in an organization are
required to meet certain criteria, then
meeting those criteria must
progress. If we ask citizen to trust
institutions then institutions must
demonstrate that their worth has value
and that their commitments endure.
The rule that applies today cannot be
different tomorrow simply because the
balance of powers has changed and a
commitment undertaken cannot be a
temporary political convenience. It must
be a foundation on which people can plan
their future. We ask our citizens to
believe in cooperation, in good
neighborly relations, in compromises,
and in mutual respect. We tell them that
lasting peace is worth more than a
short-term political victory. That
respecting agreements is a sign of
strength and wisdom and that it is the
right thing to do, not a sign of
weakness. The European and Euroatlantic
integration means accepting rules that
apply equally to all. But
that argument becomes much harder to
sustain when citizens see that in
international relations. Principle
sometimes gives way to power. that
criteria can change while the process is
already underway or that some are
expected to demonstrate consistency that
others do not always demand of
themselves.
We cannot tell people trust the rules
when they can see that the rules do not
apply equally. We cannot convince them
that compromise is a virtue if every
compromise produces a new demand. And we
cannot expect trust in international
institutions. If citizens come to
believe that their fate is created more
often by the political weight of their
state than by the strength of an agreed
principle. This is a question of
legitimacy
because our our authority as elected
leaders does not derive from the office
itself. It deres from the people who
elect us, who hold us to account and who
every day compare what we tell them with
what they see. And today
they see more than ever before. We live
in an age in which transformation
travels around the world in a second.
Never before has humanity had access to
so much knowledge. But never before has
it been exposed to so much manipulation,
halftruths, fabricated images,
propaganda and organized disinformation.
That is precisely why politics is
entering a new more difficult and more
complex era. Our task is not longer
simply to inform our citizens. We must
earn their trust. It is not enough to
tell them what is true. We must build
institutions they can trust when the
truth is uncomfortable for everyone. It
is not enough to speak to them about
values. We must show that those values
have meaning and carry cost even when
defending them requires patience,
political capital or choosing the more
difficult path.
We are called upon to convince our
societies that cooperation is better
than isolation. That rule of law is
better than unilateral behavior, that
compromise is better than conflict, and
that institutions are better than rule
of sheer force. But for the conviction
to carry weight, we ourselves must be
consistent. Values are not sustained by
speeches. They are sustained when they
are upheld precisely at the moment when
it is easiest to abandon them and many
may be greatest challenges of our time.
The world is changing at extraordinary
speed. The centers of power are
shifting. Technology is changing.
Economic relations are changing.
Security doctrines are changing.
Alliances are changing. Histories
accelerating once again. In such a
periods, there is always a temptation to
declare that old principles are no
longer practical, that the law must
adapt to power, that values are a luxury
that can wait until the crisis has
passed.
But that is precisely when we need them
most. Because if in times of change we
abandon the rules that protected us in
times of stability, we will not gain
greater freedom, we will inherit a world
in which every subsequent decision
depends on who has more power at that
particular moment. And such a world is
especially dangerous for small size
states. That is why our duty as leaders
is not to promise our people a world
without injustice, without
disappointment and without conflict
interests. Such a world does not exist.
Our duty is far more demanding. To
preserve fate in the rules even when it
is a clear that the rules are being
broken. To defend cooperation even when
confrontation appears more popular. To
sustain trust in institutions. No by
asking people to look less closely and
ask fewer questions but by making
institutions more worthy of their trust.
and not to allow disappointment with the
imperfections of the international order
to lead us towards something far worse.
A world in which there is no order at
all. That in my view is one of the
greatest political and moral
responsibilities of our generation. It
applies to the international system and
it applies to Europe. We will not
abandon the European idea because the
European path has been difficult. The
European Union remains for us our
natural political, economical and
institutional home and we have to work
to do at home. We must strengthen the
rule of law, build more effective
institutions, build a more competitive
economy and strengthen our citizens
confidence in their own state. That is
our responsibility and we will not shift
it to Brussels. At the same time, we
expect European integration to remain a
merit-based process based on measurable
criteria, not a process in which
bilateral issues can continually move
the goalposts. We are not asking for an
easier path. We are asking for a path
governed by rules. We are not asking for
lower standards. We are asking for
standards to remain standards. This is
equally important for Europe's
credibility at a time when its
geopolitical weight will increasingly
depend on its ability to translate its
commitments into the tangible political
outcome and on its resolve to uphold the
values it exposes and to remain
steadfast in advancing them despite the
many challenges it face.
Excellencies,
the future international order will not
be shaped only on battlefields or in
diplomatic halls. It will be also shaped
in laboratories, in schools, in
factories, in energy grids, in data
centers, and in the ability of societies
to make sense of the changes that
technology is bringing. Artificial
intelligence is not longer a subject of
the future. It is infrastructure for
today, for the present. Today the world
is once again recognizing the values of
resilience,
of reliable energy, of infrastructure,
of diversified transport routes, of
nearby and trusted supply chains. For
us, the intensify development of
corridor 8 and corridor 10 is a part of
broader European vision
to better connect the Adriatic, Yunian,
the Black Sea, the Asian and Central
Europe to provide goods, energy and
people with more roots and greater
connectivity and to ensure that the
region becomes interconnected in the
infrastructure rather than remaining on
the political geopolitical periphery.
Our geography does not have to be our
destiny. It can be our advantage if we
build the institutions and
infrastructure that transform our
geographical position into connectivity.
At the same time, we must also approach
migration definitely. Migration begins
where there is no security, no
employment, no education, no access to
water, no prospects or no confidence
that tomorrow will be better than today.
It is not simply a matter of borders.
Responsibly policy must bring together
security, human dignity, development and
the real needs of labor markets. Climate
policy too will have to become more
grounded in reality. The green
transition is essential. But if we make
it social unsustainable, we will lose
the political support that is necessary
to implement it. If we make it
technologically dependent on handful of
sources, we will create a new challenges
while addressing old ones. If we expect
poorer countries to move at the same
pace without providing them with equal
access to capital and technology, we
will create injustice instead of a
transition. That is why future climate
policy must at the same time be
environmental policy, economic policy
and social policy. Mr. President,
all of these bring us back to the
central theme of this session. Trust.
Trust is not a sentiment that can be
created by adopting a resolution. It is
an outcome. It is built when an
institution delivers on the purpose for
which was established. That is why
reform of United Nations is necessary so
that the organization can become more
capable
so that it can deliver greater results
and certainly not to replace the
responsibility of national states but to
act where collective action is needed.
Multilateralism does not begin in New
York. It begins when the quality of the
states that came to New York.
Excellencies, we are a smalls size
country, but we refuse to let the
smallalness of our territory define the
scale of our ambition. Our ambition is
to become a serious state. A state that
its allies can trust. A state in which
young people can plan their future. A
state that respects the diversity and
multicultural character of its society.
A state confident enough to defend its
own identity without denying the
identity of the others. A state that
knows its history but is not imprisoned
by it. And a state that does not expect
others to build it in its place.
That to me is modern sovereignity, not
isolation capability. This year,
Secretary General Antonio Gutes reminded
us on the charter begins with the
worlds. We the peoples and he added,
"Not we powerful, not we the victors."
In those words lies the reason why
smallsized European country continues to
believe in this organization even when
it is disappointed by it. Because the
alternative to a world governed by rules
is not a world in which everyone is
free. It is a world in which the
strongest are the freest and everyone
else depends on their goodwill. Such a
world may appear effective for a moment
but it is never stable. Some decades
ago, the United Nations came to our
country with a new idea that the
international community does not have to
wait for a violence to begin before it
acts. Today, we once again need to same
political wisdom. We must not wait for a
technology to create new inequalities
before we establish rules. We must not
wait for young people to live before we
build societies in which they see a
future worth staying for. We must not
wait for institutions to lose all public
trust before we reform them. And we must
not wait for the world to become fully
divided into opposing blocks before we
rediscover the values of a dialogue.
That child with whom I began will be 14
years old when the world enters in 2014.
None of us today can promise that child
a peaceful world, nor a world without
crisis, nor a world without competition.
But we can leave that child something
else. A world in which power is not the
only argument. A world in which
knowledge is not the privilege of you. A
world in which alliances create security
rather than new lines of fear. A world
in which technology serves humanity. A
world in which a small state has the
right to the same dignity to the same
rules at the same voice as a great
powers. That is the promise worth
renewing. Not because we are naive about
the world as it is, but because we are
realistic enough to understand what
happens when the world is left to power
alone. Macedonians and the Macedonian
citizens will share their burden of
responsibility. Thank you so much for
your attention.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the president of the government of
the Republic of North Macedonia.
